6 sections 2021 – 2026 timespan Updated Aug 2026

Before the term existed

Why robots needed language at all

For most of deep learning's robotics era, a policy learned one narrow skill from one narrow dataset — behavior cloning: watch a human teleoperate a task a few hundred times, copy the mapping from camera pixels to motor commands. It worked, but it didn't generalize — a policy trained to pick up a red block had no idea what to do with a blue one, let alone a spoken instruction it hadn't seen verbatim.

The fix came from outside robotics: large vision and language models already understood the world in a way no robot dataset could teach from scratch. The four works below are the ones that first plugged that outside knowledge into a robot's decision loop.

2021

CLIPort

Fuses CLIP's semantic "what" with TransporterNets' spatial "where," letting a tabletop manipulator follow open language from only a few demonstrations.

2021

BC-Z

Large-scale behavior cloning conditioned on language and video task embeddings, aimed squarely at zero-shot transfer to unseen tasks.

2022

SayCan

An LLM (PaLM) decomposes an open instruction into a sequence of affordance-grounded skills; the LLM plans, separately-learned policies execute. Not end-to-end.

2023

VoxPoser

An LLM and a VLM jointly compose 3D value maps that steer a classical motion planner — zero-shot, with no action-labeled training data at all.

SayCan's success showed that an LLM's world-knowledge could ground open-ended language into robot affordances — which raised the obvious next question: what if the language model and the motor-control policy were the same network?

2022 – 2024

The lineage

This is the chain of models that made "vision-language-action" a category with its own name — each one answering a gap the last one left open.

Dec 2022

RT-1

Google Research — FiLM-EfficientNet-B3 + Transformer
A 35M-parameter transformer trained on 130,000 real robot episodes, outputting discrete action tokens. The first VLA-shaped model built at genuine scale rather than lab scale.
Scaled up into RT-2
Jul 2023

RT-2

Google DeepMind — PaLI-X (55B) / PaLM-E (12B)
Co-fine-tunes a web-scale vision-language model on robot data and web data at once, representing actions as text tokens the VLM already knows how to emit. Showed emergent chain-of-thought reasoning about actions no robot dataset had ever demonstrated.
Establishes the "VLM backbone + action tokens" template pi0 and OpenVLA both inherit
Oct 2023

Open X-Embodiment / RT-X

Google DeepMind + 34 institutions
Pools 60 existing datasets across 22 robot embodiments into one shared corpus, and shows training across embodiments transfers positively rather than just averaging out.
Becomes the default pretraining corpus for nearly everything that follows
May 2024

Octo

UC Berkeley et al. — Transformer + diffusion action head, ~93M params
The first fully open-source generalist policy, trained on 800,000 Open X-Embodiment trajectories. Swaps discrete action tokens for a diffusion head that outputs continuous motion directly.
Sets the continuous-action-head precedent pi0's flow matching later refines
Jun 2024

OpenVLA

Stanford / Berkeley / Google et al. — Prismatic-7B (Llama-2 + SigLIP + DINOv2)
A 7B open-source VLA fine-tuned on 970,000 Open X-Embodiment episodes, outperforming the much larger RT-2-X on standard benchmarks. Still the field's most-cited open baseline.
Physical Intelligence forms and ships pi0 four months later

Oct 2024 – Apr 2025

Physical Intelligence, in depth

Physical Intelligence's models are the ones actually deployed in front-line robot fleets today, so they're worth more than a timeline entry — here's what's inside each one.

π0

Oct 2024

A single transformer with two weight sets sharing one attention stack: a pretrained open vision-language model handles seeing and reading, and a much smaller "action expert" handles moving. The action expert is trained with flow matching — the same family of technique behind modern image generators — learning to transform random noise into a coherent burst of future motion.

PaliGemma, 3B params
Action expert
Flow matching, 300M params

FAST tokenizer

Jan 2025

A parallel line of work asks: does a VLA need a separate flow-matching head at all? FAST compresses a continuous action sequence in the frequency domain (a DCT-based scheme, the same math behind JPEG compression) into a short run of discrete tokens — small enough that a plain autoregressive language model can predict them like the next word in a sentence. Training an autoregressive pi0-FAST this way is roughly 5× faster than training the flow-matching version, at the cost of the smoother, more continuous motion a dedicated diffusion-style head tends to produce at high control frequencies.

π0.5

Apr 2025

π0's open question was generalization: trained homes, trained kitchens, trained objects. π0.5's entire premise is working somewhere it has never seen — an unfamiliar kitchen, an unfamiliar bedroom — from one spoken command like "put the dishes away." It gets there by co-training on four data types at once, and by splitting inference into two stages instead of one.

May 2025 – Apr 2026

What came after π0.5

Two fixes to how π0.5 trains and runs, then two genuine successor models. In order:

May 2025

Knowledge Insulation

Physical Intelligence
Bolting an untrained action expert onto a pretrained VLM and fine-tuning end-to-end lets action-loss gradients leak back into the backbone, quietly eroding the language and vision competence it arrived with. The fix is a stop-gradient between the two — insulating the backbone from the action expert's training signal. Result: faster training, faster inference, and a policy that still follows language well.
Jun 2025

Real-Time Chunking (RTC)

Physical Intelligence — NeurIPS 2025
Action chunks create a seam: by the time the next 50-step chunk finishes computing, the robot has already burned through part of the current one, producing a jerk at the boundary. RTC starts computing the next chunk before the current one ends, treating the tail of the running chunk as a soft constraint — an inpainting problem, not a from-scratch prediction — so the seam disappears. Sub-100ms reactivity, no loss of long-horizon coherence.
executing chunk next chunk, computed early & blended
Nov 2025

π*0.6 — RECAP

Physical Intelligence — 5B backbone
Pure imitation learning has a structural flaw: one small mistake nudges the robot into a state its demonstrations never covered, and errors compound from there. RECAP (RL with Experience & Corrections via Advantage-conditioned Policies) tackles that directly in three stages — offline RL pretraining, fine-tuning on expert demonstrations, then on-robot learning that mixes live human corrections with reinforcement learning from the robot's own trial outcomes. Espresso-making and box-assembly throughput roughly doubled; laundry-folding generalized to 50 novel items never demonstrated; over 90% success across extended, unattended runs.
Apr 2026

π0.7

Physical Intelligence — current, as of this writing
Framed as "steerable": it takes correction not just as language but as visual subgoals, metadata, and other control signals describing how to do something, not only what. The headline capabilities are emergent rather than architected — recombining known skills to solve tasks it was never directly trained on, transferring zero-shot to new robot morphologies (folding laundry on a UR5e arm with no training data for that hardware at all), and absorbing step-by-step verbal coaching live. Physical Intelligence attributes this to training-data diversity and a richer prompting schema, not a larger backbone.
verified

There is no "π1." The lineage is strictly π0 → π0.5 → π0.6 / π*0.6 → π0.7. Several low-quality aggregator sites surfaced fabricated release names and dates during research for this page (including one inventing an unrelated "π0.7 air fryer" product); those were discarded in favor of Physical Intelligence's own blog and the corresponding arXiv papers.

Under the hood

The mechanism, precisely

Everything above described what each model does. This is how — the actual objectives, attention pattern, and inference-time procedures, pulled from the papers rather than paraphrased into vagueness. Notation follows each paper as published, including where π0's own convention runs backwards from what you'd expect.

Flow matching, as π0 actually runs it

arXiv 2410.24164

An action chunk is a window of continuous future joint/end-effector targets. π0 doesn't predict it directly — it learns a vector field that morphs Gaussian noise into that chunk over a handful of integration steps, conditioned on the current observation o_t (the VLM's encoding of image + language + robot state).

Derivation — noise to action, in four lines

τ runs 0→1 from noise to clean data — the reverse of typical diffusion-time convention, as published.

01
Atτ = τ·At + (1−τ)·ε,  ε ~ 𝒩(0, I)

Linear interpolation between the clean action chunk At and Gaussian noise ε. At τ=0 you have pure noise; at τ=1, the real action chunk.

02
u(Atτ | At) = ε − At

The target velocity: a constant vector field pointing from data back toward the noise sample that generated it, along that same straight line.

03
Lτ(θ) = 𝔼 ‖ vθ(Atτ, ot) − u(Atτ|At) ‖²

Train the action expert vθ to regress that velocity, at randomly sampled noise levels τ, conditioned on the scene.

04
Atτ+δ = Atτ + δ·vθ(Atτ, ot)

At inference: forward Euler integration, δ = 0.1, 10 steps from pure noise to an executable action chunk — cheap enough to run well under the control loop's budget.

Fig. 2b — line 04, running live: 40 samples of one action dimension, τ=0 → τ=1

τ = 0.0 step 0 / 10 grey = noise sample · orange = current Atτ

Pretraining spanned 7 robot configs — single and bimanual UR5e, Franka, bimanual Trossen, bimanual ARX/AgileX, mobile Trossen/ARX, mobile Fibocom — across 68 tasks, plus OXE, Bridge v2, and DROID.

One transformer, two experts, a blockwise mask

architecture

The VLM backbone and the action expert aren't two separate networks bolted together — they're one transformer, one attention operation per layer, with two separate weight sets (backbone width 2048, action expert width 1024, ~300M params) applied to three token blocks: image+language, proprioceptive state, and action. A blockwise-causal mask keeps information flowing only forward through that list — full attention within a block, but a block never attends to one that comes after it.

Fig. 3 — attention mask (row attends-to column)

Row 1 — image + language: attends only to itself Row 2 — proprioceptive state: adds image + language Row 3 — action tokens: attends to everything before it, plus itself

Action chunking's other half: temporal ensembling

ACT, 2023

Chunking alone would mean re-planning only every 50 steps. In practice, a new chunk is predicted at every timestep, and the overlapping predictions for the same future instant are blended — no retraining required, purely an inference-time trick.

01
at = Σᵢ wi·ât(i),   wi = e−m·i / Σⱼ e−m·j

ât(i) is timestep t's action as predicted from i steps ago. Older predictions get exponentially less weight — smoother motion than committing to one chunk wholesale, at the cost of extra forward passes.

Fig. 4 — four overlapping predictions blending into one executed path

w₀=0.55 · w₁=0.30 · w₂=0.11 · w₃=0.04

RTC: chunk boundaries as an inpainting problem

arXiv 2506.07339

Rather than temporal ensembling's blend-after-the-fact, RTC changes what gets generated in the first place. The prefix of actions already committed to the robot is frozen outright. For the remaining overlap window, a soft mask that decays exponentially with distance from that frozen prefix is added as a guidance term inside the same flow-matching denoising process — pulling the new chunk toward consistency with the old one without hard-constraining it, so the seam disappears without a jerk in either direction.

Fig. 5 — guidance weight across the overlap window

Knowledge Insulation: where exactly the gradient stops

arXiv 2505.23705

The insulation isn't a blanket freeze of the backbone — it's surgical, applied only inside the cross-attention terms where the action expert reads from the backbone:

01
Qa(Xa)·sg(Kb(Xb)ᵀ)  and  Pab·sg(Vb(Xb))

sg(·) is stop-gradient. The action expert (a) still reads the backbone's (b) keys and values in full — it just can't push gradients back through them. The backbone keeps training on its own FAST-tokenized next-action-token loss the whole time, as a representation-learning signal in its own right.

Fig. 6 — where the gradient does and doesn't flow

Effect: matches π0-FAST's training speed — π0 needs 7.5× more training steps without this — while running inference at ~10Hz vs π0-FAST's ~1.3Hz, and scoring 96.0% on LIBERO-90.

RECAP: conditioning on your own advantage

π*0.6

The advantage-conditioning is decision-transformer-style: the policy is trained on both good and bad actions, each tagged with the change in a learned value function they produced. At deployment, you simply prompt it to emit high-advantage behavior. Physical Intelligence hasn't published the offline-RL algorithm behind stage one of the recipe — treat that specific piece as undisclosed rather than inferring an architecture for it.

Fig. 7 — RECAP's three training stages

IndustReal: four fixes for sim-to-real assembly

arXiv 2305.17110

A deeper look at the case study introduced under Try It Yourself. Prior sim-to-real work on assembly leaned on crutches — human demonstrations, a hand-built baseline motion plan, or a phase of real-world fine-tuning after transfer — because contact-rich insertion punishes the two assumptions the rest of robot RL gets away with: that the simulator's contact physics are close enough to real, and that a policy trained blind to contact forces will behave sensibly once it's touching something. IndustReal's claim is that a policy can go from simulation to a real Franka arm with none of those crutches, provided four specific failure modes are each patched individually.

The RL setup itself is deliberately plain: PPO (via the rl-games implementation), an asymmetric actor-critic — the actor only ever sees joint angles and gripper/object/target poses, because joint velocities and torques are too noisy to trust on real hardware, while the critic (which never has to leave simulation) is allowed to see velocities too, since a better-informed value function speeds up training without costing anything at deployment. Actions are incremental pose deltas a = [Δx; Δq] rather than absolute targets, so the same network shape covers peg, gear, and connector insertion without per-task retuning. And the low-level controller is Franka's own task-space impedance (TSI) mode, chosen over the more common operational-space control specifically because OSC needs an accurate dynamics model to compute torques from — exactly the kind of model contact-rich sim-to-real can't assume it has, while Franka ships a production-grade TSI implementation for free.

None of that is unusual for robot RL. What actually made assembly work is four narrow, separately-motivated fixes layered on top:

1 — SAPU. A rigid-body simulator's collision solver is not perfectly rigid: a plug moving fast enough can briefly phase a few tenths of a millimeter into a socket's mesh before the solver pushes it back out. That's numerically harmless in simulation, but it's also exactly the kind of trajectory a reward-maximizing policy will happily learn to exploit — barrel through the wall of the hole a little, get "inserted" a step early, collect the reward. A policy trained that way has learned that sockets are slightly compliant. Real sockets aren't, so it just collides and fails. SAPU's fix is to make interpenetration visible to the reward function instead of invisible to it.

SAPU — stop rewarding the policy for phasing through geometry

01
dipmax = maxi penetration(T·pi, socket),  i = 1…1000

Every episode, 1,000 points sampled on and inside the plug mesh are transformed into the socket's frame and run through a GPU-based interpenetration check, in parallel across every simulated environment, giving one worst-case penetration depth per rollout.

02
weight = 1 − tanh(dipmax / εd)  ·   discard episode if dipmax > εip = 1mm

Two separate mechanisms, tested individually and together. Filter throws the whole episode's return away outright once penetration crosses a hard 1mm line — a trajectory that egregious gets zero credit, full stop. Weight is softer: every episode's return gets scaled down continuously by how deep it phased through, via a tanh that saturates smoothly instead of a hard cliff. Neither alone worked as well as both together — Filter-and-Weight reached 84.9–87.6% real-world success, ahead of either mechanism run in isolation.

2 — SDF-based reward. A sparse reward — success or nothing — gives an RL policy almost no signal at the start of training, because a randomly-acting arm essentially never lands a peg in a 0.5mm-clearance hole by chance. The obvious fix is a dense reward that scores "how close," but the naive version of that — straight-line distance from plug to target — actively lies once contact starts: after the peg's tip has touched the socket's rim, the shortest path to inserted usually runs through the socket wall, so a policy chasing straight-line distance gets pulled toward exactly the collision behavior SAPU is trying to discourage. The fix is to measure distance using the target's own geometry instead of a straight line to a point.

SDF reward — dense feedback shaped like the socket's own geometry

01
reward = −log( (1/N) Σᵢ φ(xi) )

φ is the socket's signed-distance field at the target pose, precomputed once offline. xi are 1,000 fixed points on the plug's surface, transformed to the plug's current pose every step and looked up against that field — so the reward already "knows" the socket's exact shape, chamfers and all, rather than measuring distance to one abstract target point.

02
SDF: 88.60%  vs.  keypoint: 15.4–54.2%  vs.  Chamfer distance: 1.8%

The reward's shape was the single largest lever in the whole paper. A handful of hand-picked keypoints gets partway there but is inconsistent (15.4–54.2%, evidently sensitive to exactly which points get picked). Chamfer distance — a completely standard shape-similarity loss everywhere else in geometric deep learning — collapses to 1.8% success as an RL reward here, presumably for the same reason plain Euclidean distance fails: it stops pointing toward "inserted" the moment the geometry gets involved.

3 — Sampling-Based Curriculum. Assembly RL is normally curriculum-trained by starting the peg already inside the hole and slowly raising the starting height as the policy improves — but a fixed schedule can't tell the difference between a policy that's ready to advance and one that's having a temporarily bad run, and once it's advanced it never goes back. SBC replaces the schedule with a feedback loop against the policy's own recent performance.

SBC — a curriculum that reacts to the policy instead of a fixed schedule

01
zlow ← zlow + Δzi  if pn > 80%   |   zlow − Δzd  if pn < 10%   |   zlow  otherwise

The initial plug height for each new episode is sampled uniformly from a band [zlow, zhigh] rather than fixed. zhigh stays put at 10mm above the hole; zlow starts 10mm below the hole's top edge (i.e. training starts with the plug already partly engaged) and only moves in response to the policy's trailing success rate pn — climbing by Δzi=5mm when it's winning easily (>80%), retreating by the smaller Δzd=3mm when it's struggling (<10%), holding still in between.

02
SBC: 88.6% success, 96.6% engagement  vs.  fixed schedule: 32.4%  vs.  no curriculum: 66.8%

The asymmetry (advance in bigger steps than it retreats) is deliberate — it biases the curriculum toward getting harder over the course of training while still leaving an escape hatch, and that combination beats both a monotonic fixed schedule and no curriculum at all by a wide margin.

4 — Policy-Level Action Integrator. The first three fixes all happen during training, in simulation. PLAI is the odd one out: it changes nothing about training and is applied purely when the already-trained policy is running on the real arm. Simulation dynamics are idealized — no unmodeled stiction, no gravity-compensation error — so a policy trained there has no reason to have learned to correct for the small systematic tracking errors those introduce on real hardware. Retraining with randomized dynamics is the standard answer, but IndustReal explicitly avoids dynamics randomization elsewhere in the pipeline (see below); PLAI gets the correction for free at deployment time instead, with an idea borrowed straight from classical control.

PLAI — a PID-flavored fix applied only at deployment, never during training

01
standard: st+1d = st ⊕ at     PLAI: st+1d = std ⊕ at = s0d ⊕ Σi=0T−1 ai

The standard way to execute a policy's output is to add its commanded delta at onto the current measured state st — which means any steady-state tracking error just gets re-measured and baked into the next command, never corrected. PLAI instead accumulates every action against its own running commanded target std, ignoring where the arm actually ended up — mathematically the same move as an integral term in a PID loop, which is exactly why it cancels the same class of steady-state error. A "leaky" variant caps how much can accumulate, so the integrator doesn't wind up into a runaway command while the plug is jammed mid-contact.

02
PLAI: ≈2mm real-world tracking error  vs.  Franka's native controller: 4.45mm

No retraining, no simulator change, no extra real-world data — applied at inference time only, it more than halves real-world tracking error on its own, and holds ≈2mm consistently in simulation whether the test condition is ideal, frictional, or has bad gravity compensation.

What all four have in common: nowhere in this pipeline does the robot see a real demonstration, a scripted motion plan, or a fine-tuning phase after transfer. The only real-world contact this policy has before deployment is the URDF-fidelity work under Try It Yourself — and, deliberately, not randomized dynamics. Initial end-effector and object poses are randomized over a large spatial range during training, and the insertion policies get observation noise added, but friction and mass are left at their corrected, physically-measured values rather than sampled across a wide range. At test time on the real robot, the only injected perturbation is ±2mm of noise added to the target-pose observation, to check the policy hasn't just memorized one exact geometry.

Collect demonstrations

Teleoperate your arm through the task via lerobot's leader-follower recording flow (or generate rollouts in sim), saved as a LeRobotDataset — synchronized images, robot state, and actions in one format every policy in the zoo reads. Neither openpi's nor lerobot's docs state a minimum episode count for fine-tuning an existing checkpoint onto a new task — that number genuinely isn't published, so treat any figure you see elsewhere as a community rule of thumb, not a documented requirement.

Fine-tune from a base checkpoint

Start from whichever released checkpoint is closest to your setup — π0.5-base for a fresh task, or a specialized ALOHA/DROID/LIBERO checkpoint if your hardware matches one. Fine-tuning from a pretrained generalist, not training from scratch, is the entire point of a foundation-model-shaped VLA: the cross-embodiment pretraining has already done the expensive part.

Close the sim-to-real gap

π0.5's own generalization strategy is co-training on heterogeneous real-world data — multiple robots, web data, verbal instructions, subtask labels — not heavy synthetic domain randomization. That means the highest-leverage move is usually collecting real demonstrations on your own hardware rather than perfecting a simulator. If you do go the sim2real route, domain randomization (textures, lighting, camera pose; friction, mass) is the standard technique across the wider Isaac/MuJoCo ecosystem — but it isn't wired into openpi or lerobot out of the box, so you'd be building that layer yourself.

Case study — IndustReal, RSS 2023

A different paradigm worth knowing, if the task is contact-rich enough that imitation learning struggles with it: not a pretrained VLA fine-tuned from demonstrations, but a from-scratch reinforcement-learning policy trained entirely in NVIDIA's Isaac Gym and transferred to a real Franka arm for sub-millimeter peg and gear insertion. Full methodology, with equations and results — The Mechanism, above.

Policy update
SAPU — simulation-aware policy update
Reward
SDF-based contact reward
Curriculum
Sampling-based curriculum (SBC)
Hardware
Franka arm, custom-corrected URDF

The unglamorous part matters as much as the algorithm: they rebuilt Franka's URDF against the official spec sheet and stripped out the arbitrary dissipative terms simulators add by default — the physical fidelity of the model you're transferring from turned out to be as load-bearing as anything RL-specific. Training from scratch: 8–10 hours for peg insertion, 18–20 hours for gears.

this is RL trained per-task from scratch in sim, not a fine-tuned foundation model — complementary evidence for the sim2real branch above, not an alternative reading of π0.5's own co-training approach. Tang et al., arXiv 2305.17110, RSS 2023 · code & docs: isaac-sim/IsaacGymEnvs

Evaluate honestly

Run N trials per task and report the raw success rate — not a cherry-picked demo. If your policy's inference latency is fighting your control loop, this is where RTC earns its keep: it's already documented in lerobot for exactly this problem.

unconfirmed

Three numbers this page deliberately does not state, because no credible source does: the offline-RL algorithm inside RECAP's stage one, a minimum episode count for fine-tuning openpi checkpoints, and ALOHA 2's kit price (only the single-arm ALOHA Solo's $8,999.95 is published). If you find a primary source for any of these, that's worth more than a plausible-sounding guess.

Reference

Glossary

VLM backbone
The pretrained vision-language model — PaliGemma, PaLI-X, Llama-2+SigLIP — that a VLA repurposes for robot control, supplying visual grounding and language understanding before any robot-specific training begins.
Action chunking
Predicting a short run of future actions (e.g. 50 timesteps) in one pass instead of one action at a time — smoother, more temporally consistent motion, at the cost of reacting a beat slower to sudden changes.
Flow matching vs. diffusion vs. autoregressive tokenization
Three ways to turn a network's output into motion. Diffusion and flow matching both refine random noise into a plausible action sequence step by step — flow matching learns a straighter path between the two, so it needs fewer refinement steps. Autoregressive tokenization (FAST) instead compresses actions into discrete symbols and predicts them one at a time, the same way a language model predicts words.
End-effector vs. joint-space action
Whether the model targets the gripper's position in 3D space (end-effector space — transfers more easily across different arm geometries) or the angle of every individual motor (joint-space — more precise, but tied to one specific hardware layout).
Cross-embodiment training
Training one model on data from many different robots — different arms, grippers, sensors, wheeled bases, bimanual rigs — so it learns motion patterns that transfer, rather than overfitting to one machine.
Co-training
Mixing robot action data with non-robot data — web images, captions, human video, verbal instructions — in the same training run, so the model keeps broad competence instead of narrowing to only what's in the robot dataset.
Imitation learning vs. reinforcement learning
Imitation learning copies expert demonstrations directly, but small errors compound once the robot drifts outside what was demonstrated. Reinforcement learning lets the robot try, fail, and improve from its own outcomes — correcting that drift, at the cost of needing far more real-world trial and error.
Zero-/few-shot generalization
Handling a new task or environment with no (zero-shot) or a handful (few-shot) of task-specific examples, leaning on what the model already absorbed during broader pretraining.

Primary sources: Physical Intelligence's research blog (pi.website/blog) and the corresponding arXiv papers for π0 (2410.24164), FAST (2501.09747), and π0.5 (2504.16054); Google DeepMind, NVIDIA, and Figure AI's own announcements for the field-today comparisons.
